image_ref.observation: the plan labelled ADAMS CO. COURT HO. is filled red (brick) and carries the numeral 2 at its north-west corner; a small yellow (frame) square stands inside the plan near its north end; a broken line along the west side; a circle (slate or tin roof) at the east side; the printed key of the sheet: buildings coloured red are brick, yellow frame, blue stone; a numeral is the number of stories; x is a shingle roof, a circle a slate or tin roof; a broken line near a building is a wood cornice

value: a steeple containing a bell and a town clock
quote: strong and solidly built from foun- dation stone to turret, commodious and well appointed in its court room and of- fices, with strong fire-proof vaults, and crowned with steeple containing bell and town clock
basis: the History of 1886 describes the building in the present tense ("crowned with steeple containing bell and town clock"); it does not date the clock; the town clock "now in the cupola" is the gift of H. D. Wattles of January 1868 (the other row); Tillie Pierce heard "the Court House clock" strike in 1863 (a memoir of 1889)

value.text: the elegant town clock, a gift of H. D. Wattles to the borough, now in the cupola of the court house

quote: January 27, 1868 — Mr. H. D. Wattles presented to the borough, as a free gift from him, the elegant town clock, now in the cupola of the court house
basis: an addition of 1868 reported in 1886; it is not in the July 1863 state; whether the building had an earlier clock in July 1863 is not stated by this text (the History of 1886 says the steeple of 1859 contained a town clock; Tillie Pierce, writing in 1889, heard the Court House clock in 1863)

detail: Captain L. B. Norton, Signal Officer: on 1 July a station of observation was established first on the college and subsequently on the court-house in Gettysburg, reporting to General Howard on Cemetery Hill; the sentence does not give the hour

detail: Daniel Skelly (memoir of 1932 in the Slyder guide, p. 18): the court house, with three churches and the school house on High Street, received the wounded of the First Corps until full; he carried water into the court house; the wounded of 1 July were first laid on the floor of the McCurdy warehouse (not in this group)
